Matrix Multiplication from Polynomial Packings: A Constructive and Elementary Proof of \(\omega\le 9/4\)

Rafael Pass<sup>∗</sup>

**Abstract**

We give a self-contained constructive proof that the matrix multiplication exponent satisfies \(\omega\le 9/4\). This bound was recently claimed by OpenAI [Ope26a] through non-constructive arguments in Strassen’s asymptotic spectral framework, counting exact scalar arithmetic operations over the complex numbers. We explicitly construct a Strassen-style matrix multiplication identity and obtain the bound by ordinary block recursion. For every \(\gamma>0\), the resulting algorithm multiplies two \(n\times n\) integer matrices using \(O(n^{9/4+\gamma})\) integer arithmetic operations.

<sup>∗</sup>Pearl Research, Cornell Tech, Technion, TAU

## 1 Introduction

The exponent \(\omega\) of matrix multiplication is the infimum of all \(\tau\) such that two \(n\times n\) matrices can be multiplied with \(O(n^\tau)\) arithmetic operations. Strassen \[Str69\] showed \(\omega\le log_27<2.81\). Later bounds follow a scheme developed by Bini, Capovani, Romani, and Lotti \[BCRL79, Bin80\], Schönhage \[Sch81\], and Strassen \[Str87\]. An explicit identity computes several products together, possibly with an error that vanishes with a parameter. Combining identifies amplifies the saving, and the resulting independent products give a bound on \(\omega\). Refinements of Strassen’s laser method, starting from the identity of Coppersmith and Winograd \[CW90\], reached \(\omega<2.371339\) \[ADV<sup>+</sup>25\] and \(\omega<2.371177\) \[DEK<sup>+</sup>26\].

OpenAI recently claimed \(\omega\le 9/4\) \[Ope26a\], following a companion bound \(\omega<2.258\) \[Ope26b\], starting from identities for polynomial multiplication. Their theorem is stated for _exact arithmetic_ over the complex numbers, charging unit cost per scalar operation. Their proof uses Strassen’s asymptotic spectrum \[Str88\], an algebraic and topological framework for comparing bilinear maps through numerical invariants. Concavity strengthens inequalities for these invariants; spectral duality then converts them into the exponent bound. Their argument establishes the exponent bound without explicitly constructing the corresponding algorithms.

We give an explicit, constructive algorithm reaching the same bound using integer arithmetic throughout; furthermore, our construction is self-contained. Our starting point is the three-for-one polynomial degeneration of \[Ope26a, Lemma 4.2\]. We generalize it to a (_c_+2)-for-_c_ polynomial packing and nexy use our (_c_+2)-for-_c_ gadget, together with tensoring, to construct a Strassen-style identity: a fixed \(v\times v\) block matrix product can be computed using _r_ products of linear combinations of its blocks, with log_<sub>v</sub>r_ arbitrarily close to 9/4. This replaces the usual _v_<sup>3</sup> block products by _r_, just as Strassen replaces eight by seven. Applying the fixed identity recursively then gives the exponent bound.

**Theorem 1.1.** _For every_ \(\gamma>0\)_, there is an explicit recursive algorithm that, for every positive integer n, multiplies two_ \(n\times n\) _integer matrices with_ \(O(n^{9/4+\gamma})\) _integer arithmetic operations. In particular,_ \(\omega\le 9/4\).

The algorithm remains "galactic": the constants hidden in the \(O(\cdot)\) notation are enormous.

### 1.1 Our techniques

We first introduce the notion of a _polynomial packing_ (PP): a procedure that recovers a collection of polynomial-product coefficients through linear encodings, source polynomial products, and linear decoding. Its efficiency depends on both the number and the dimensions of the source products.

#### Polynomial packing.

We now construct a (_c_+2)-for-_c_ packing modulo \(\varepsilon\), generalizing the three-for-one construction of \[Ope26a, Lemma 4.2\]. Consider univariate polynomials _A,P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P_<sub>_c_+1</sub> with matrix coefficients, where _A_ has length _a_ and each _P<sub>i</sub>_ has length _b_. Write \[_z<sup>k</sup>_\]_H_ for the coefficient matrix of _z<sup>k</sup>_ in _H_, taking coefficients outside its range to be zero. We want to compute all coefficients of the _c_+1 products _AP_<sub>1</sub>_,...,AP_<sub>_c_+1</sub>, which we call _full products_. Naively, this takes _c_+1 polynomial multiplications. We can trivially reduce the number of polynomial multiplications to _c_ by replacing _P<sub>c</sub>,P_<sub>_c_+1</sub> with _P<sub>c</sub>+z_<sup>_a+b_-1</sup>_P_<sub>_c_+1</sub>: the two products then occupy disjoint coefficient ranges and can be read off separately. But this encoded input has length _a_+2_b_-1, at least the<tbc>

combined length 2_b_ of the two original inputs. The smaller number of polynomial multiplications therefore gives no saving in the total number of input coefficients. Alternatively, we can use _c_ encoded right polynomials with just one extra coefficient each. For \(c\ge a+b-1\), set \(E_j^{(0)}=P_j-zP_{j+1},1\le j\le c.\) Each \(E_j^{(0)}\) has length _b_+1. After multiplying these polynomials by _A_, take the following telescoping sum: \(\sum_{j=1}^cz^{j-1}AE_j^{(0)}=(AP_1-zAP_2)+(zAP_2-z^2AP_3)+\cdots+(z^{c-1}AP_c-z^cAP_{c+1})\)
\(=AP_1-z^cAP_{c+1}.\) This sum is computed by adding coefficients. Writing \(W_j=AE_j^{(0)}\) and _W_ for the displayed sum, we have \([z^k]W=\sum_{j=1}^c[z^{k-j+1}]W_j\). Thus forming _W_ is a linear decoding operation. The intermediate products cancel, so the first _a+b_-1 coefficients give _AP_1, and the differences \(AE_j^{(0)}=AP_j-zAP_{j+1}\) then recover the remaining products successively. This still gives no saving in the total number of right-input coefficients: \(c(b+1)\ge(c+1)b\). But notice the _empty space_ in the combined output: _AP_1 ends before position _a+b_-1, while _zcAP__c_+1 starts at position _c_. Taking \(c\ge a+2b-1\) leaves at least _b_ zero coefficient positions between them. We use this space to obtain an additional product output, without making the encoded polynomials any longer. Introduce a polynomial _Q_ of length _a+b_-1 and write \(Q=\sum_{j=0}^{c-1}q_jz^j\), padding with zeros. Let \(\varepsilon\) be a formal parameter. Modify the encoding to \(E_j=P_j-zP_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^bq_{j-1},1\le j\le c.\) _That is, we add just one coefficient of_ \(\varepsilon Q\) _to each Ej, at position b. Each Pj ends at position b_-1_, but the shifted zP__j_+1 _already reaches position b: the added coefficient overlaps with its last coefficient._ Without Q AP1 zero coefficients -c APc+1 With EQ overlapping middle of EQ overlapping contributions shifted by zb contributions 0 a + b - 1 c = a + 2b - 1 coefficient position Figure 1: The telescoping sum before and after adding \(\varepsilon Q\), shown for _c=a_+2_b_-1. The _b_ highlighted coefficients of \(\varepsilon z^bAQ\) fill the zero gap; its remaining coefficients can overlap the endpoint products.

<tbc>By distributivity, the same shifted sum now gives

\(\sum_{j=1}^cz^{j-1}AE_j=AP_1-z^cAP_{c+1}+\varepsilon z^bAQ.\)

The coefficients at positions _a_-1_,...,a+b_-2 of \(\varepsilon AQ\), shifted by _z<sup>b</sup>_, lie entirely in the gap. Dividing them by \(\varepsilon\) recovers these coefficients of _AQ_ exactly; we call this output a _middle product_. For the full products, use the same successive decoder as before and reduce modulo \(\varepsilon\): every contribution from _Q_ vanishes. Our so-called _same-left primal packing_ therefore computes

\(\underbrace{(AP_i)_{i=1}^{c+1}}_{c+1\text{full products}}\underbrace{\big([z^k](AQ)\big)_{k=a-1}^{a+b-2}}_{1\text{middle product}}(\text{mod}\varepsilon).\)

Reduction modulo \(\varepsilon\) means taking the constant coefficient of the fully decoded result. The only division by \(\varepsilon\) is applied to the middle output, which is divisible by \(\varepsilon\), so no negative powers remain. Thus _we compute c_+2 _polynomial-product outputs modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _using c multiplications, with only one extra coefficient in each encoded right polynomial._

To see the gain and its cost, take _a=b=L_ and _c_=3_L_. The encoded polynomials then have length _L_+1=(1+3_/c)L_. In return, _c_ source products provide _c_+1 full outputs and one middle output, giving a packing gain of (_c_+2)_/c_=1+2_/c_. The additional middle window increases the number of outputs from _c_+1 to _c_+2 without increasing the source lengths. The balanced primal/dual construction below converts this improvement into an exponent saving.

We also construct and rely on a _dual_ of the above packing, which reverses the roles: it computes _c_+1 middle products and one full product modulo \(\varepsilon\) using _c_ slightly longer middle-product calls. We obtain it by exchanging and transposing the linear encoding and decoding maps. Transposition preserves the constant coefficient of the decoded map.

## Amplifying the gain: Multivariate Packing.

Running the primal and dual packings side by side gives _c_+2 full and _c_+2 middle outputs from _c_ full and _c_ middle source products. Their counts add, so the gain remains 2(_c_+2)/(2_c_)=(_c_+2)_/c_. To multiply the gain, we move to multivariate polynomials and apply the packings in separate variables. In two variables _x,y_, one primal step in _x_ and one dual step in _y_ give (_c_+2)<sup>2</sup> outputs from _c_<sup>2</sup> source products; continuing in additional variables multiplies the gain further. To see why, start with one common left polynomial _A(x,y_) of length _a_ in each variable and a \((c+2)\times(c+2)\) table of independent right polynomials _B<sub>i,j</sub>(x,y_). We want coefficients of each product _AB<sub>i,j</sub>_. For rows 1_,...,c_+1, we want Full in _x_; for the last row, Mid in _x_. For columns 1_,...,c_+1, we want Mid in _y_; for the last column, Full in _y_. Each _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ has length _b_ in a variable where we want Full and length _a+b_-1 where we want Mid. Figure 2 shows every row and column for _c_=4. For example, each of the (_c_+1)<sup>2</sup> upper-left products requests \([x^ky^\ell](AB_{i,j})\) for \(0\le k<a+b-1\) and \(a-1\le\ell<a+b-1\); its right input has lengths (_b,a+b_-1). Every column supplies the _c_+1 full-range inputs and one middle-range input needed by the primal packing in _x_. Every row supplies the _c_+1 middle-range inputs and one full-range input needed by the dual packing in _y_.

As above, take \(c\ge a+2b-1\). In each column, apply the primal encoder in _x_, viewing the coefficients as polynomials in _y_. This leaves _c_ rows, with the _y_-lengths unchanged. In each resulting row, apply the dual encoder in _y_, viewing the coefficients as polynomials in _x_. We now have a \(c\times c\) table of encoded right polynomials, each of length _b_+1 in _x_ and _a+b_ in _y_. Multiply each by _A_,<tbc>

computing all _x_-coefficients and the _y_-coefficients at exponents _a_-1_,...,a+b_-1. Apply the dual decoder in _y_, then the primal decoder in _x_.

Encoding in _x_ and then in _y_, computing the source products, and decoding in reverse order recovers all the requested outputs modulo \(\varepsilon\). This follows by applying the correctness of the two univariate packings along their separate coefficient indices.

We therefore recover (_c_+2)<sup>2</sup> outputs from _c_<sup>2</sup> source products. Furthermore, continuing this process in additional variables amplifies the compression exponentially. Use 2_d_ variables _z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z_<sub>2_d_</sub>, applying the primal packing in the first _d_ and the dual packing in the last _d_. Encode in each variable, compute the resulting products, and decode in reverse order. This gives (_c_+2)<sup>2_d_</sup> outputs from _c_<sup>2_d_</sup> source products, a compression factor of ((_c_+2)_/c_)<sup>2_d_</sup>.

There is one issue: the source products are all Full in the first _d_ variables and Mid in the last _d_, whereas the recovered outputs can have different numbers of Full and Mid directions. To obtain a recursive rule that we can apply repeatedly, we need to "end where we started": the targets must have the same form as the sources. This requires, in particular, _d_ Full and _d_ Mid directions in each target, so we keep only these outputs. For example, in the two-variable table, the yellow and green outputs have two Full or two Mid directions, respectively, so they do not qualify. The (_c_+1)<sup>2</sup> blue outputs and the single purple output have one of each: 26 of the 36 outputs when _c_=4. With 2_d_ variables, we recover at least<tbc>

\(\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}\)

<tbc>outputs of this shape.<sup>1</sup> Thus requiring this common shape costs at most a factor _d_+1 in the output count, while the compression gain grows exponentially in _d_. (Their Full and Mid directions may<tbc>

### From SL-PP to PP.

So far, the same-left polynomial packing (SL-PP) computes _w_ retained targets sharing one left input _A_. We now want independent pairs _A<sub>i</sub>,B<sub>i</sub>_. Write each right input as

\(B_i=[B_{i,0}\cdots B_{i,w-1}],\)

where the brackets denote horizontal concatenation of column blocks in every coefficient matrix. Thus group _i_ consists of the blocks of one _B<sub>i</sub>_, all multiplied by the same _A<sub>i</sub>_. We batch the _A<sub>i</sub>_ into one auxiliary univariate polynomial \(A(\xi)\) satisfying _A(i_)=_A<sub>i</sub>_. For each _i_, encode the column blocks _B<sub>i,j</sub>_ in a univariate polynomial \(B'_i(\xi)\) satisfying \(B'_i(i+\varepsilon j)=B_{i,j}\). Both encodings have degree at most _w_-1, so the requested coefficients of \(A(\xi)B'_i(\xi)\) are polynomials of degree at most 2_w_-2 in \(\xi\). We recover these polynomials by interpolation from 2_w_-1 common evaluation points. Fix one such point _k_. We need the requested coefficients of the products \(A(k)B'_0(k),\dots,A(k)B'_{w-1}(k)\). Their right inputs differ, but their left input is the single value _A(k_) of the polynomial encoding all the _A<sub>i</sub>_. Thus one application of the same-left packing computes all these products’ requested coefficients modulo \(\varepsilon\). We repeat this for each of the 2_w_-1 evaluation points; _A(k_) may change between applications. Evaluating the recovered polynomials at \(i+\varepsilon j\) gives the requested coefficients of _A<sub>i</sub>B<sub>i,j</sub>_ modulo \(\varepsilon\), since \(A(i+\varepsilon j)\equiv A_i(\mathrm{mod}\varepsilon)\).<sup>2</sup> Concatenating these output blocks recovers the requested coefficients of _A<sub>i</sub>B<sub>i</sub>_ for each _i_. (OpenAI \[Ope26a\] proves a related separation lemma using finite Fourier projection and a weight degeneration.)

### A Strassen-like identity.

Transposing the matrix products gives a row-reduction gadget. Exchanging the left-input and output roles, by transposing the corresponding encoding and decoding maps, gives an inner-dimension reduction. Combining these with the column reduction gives one gadget that reduces all three matrix dimensions simultaneously. The resulting family is ordinary matrix multiplication at _a=b_=1, is symmetric in _a,b_ under fixed coefficient permutations, and at _a=b=L_ can be computed using _O(L_<sup>6_d_</sup>) matrix multiplications. We can therefore compose a step increasing _b_ with one increasing _a_: for _d=c_<sup>3</sup>, one round increases both lengths by a factor approaching 1+3_/c_, reduces each matrix dimension by approximately (1+2_/c_)<sup>4_d_</sup>, and multiplies the number of remaining products by at most 64. The exponent approaches

\(\frac{\mathrm{log}64+6d\mathrm{log}(1+3/c)}{4d\mathrm{log}(1+2/c)}\longrightarrow\frac{9}{4}.\)

After finitely many rounds, amplification and constant-coefficient interpolation give a fixed exact rational identity with this saving. Clearing its denominators and applying ordinary block recursion gives our integer-arithmetic algorithm.

## 2 Polynomial packings

We now define packing and the two operations used to build larger packings. We then construct the univariate gadgets, combine them across variables, and give their targets independent left inputs. We first fix notation for polynomials, linear maps, and their matrix inputs.

<sup>2</sup>The formal proof replaces the original packing’s parameter by \(\varepsilon^w\), ensuring that divisions by \(\varepsilon\) in the right-input encoding leave the decoded error divisible by \(\varepsilon\).

All vector spaces and linear maps are over Q unless a formal parameter is displayed. A polynomial has _length a_ in a variable if its degree in that variable is less than _a_; for several variables, the bounds apply separately. We identify a polynomial with its coefficient list, write \([\mathbf{z}^\unknown]A\) for a coefficient, and set coefficients outside the specified bounds to zero. Input _coefficient sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times r\) mean that each coefficient of _A_ is a \(p\times q\) matrix and each coefficient of _B_ is a \(q\times r\) matrix.

For lists, a linear map has the form \(E(U)_k=\sum_ie_{ki}U_i\); we use _E(U_) and _EU_ interchangeably. The bilinear maps used for polynomial products have the form

\(F(A,B)_k=\sum_{i,j}f_{ijk}A_iB_j,f_{ijk}\in\mathbb{Q}.\) (1)

The same formula defines the map on scalars and on compatible matrix coefficients. In particular, it commutes with concatenating or splitting column blocks of _B_. The numbers _f<sub>ijk</sub>_ are its coefficient array. Each map includes its input spaces and output space in its specification.

We write \[_m_\]={1_,...,m_}, use natural logarithms, and allow constants in \(O_c(\cdot)\) to depend on _c_. An explicit construction is a finite algorithm producing its parameters and rational linear maps.

## 2.1 Packing and composition

A packing computes prescribed target maps using linear encodings, a list of source maps, and linear decoding. Keeping the two input encodings separate will allow transposition and substitution of matrix blocks.

**Definition 2.1** (Packing)**.** Let _T_ and \(S_1,\dots,S_\alpha\) be bilinear maps on specified finite-dimensional spaces. A _packing_ of _T_ using these sources consists of linear encoders _E<sub>j</sub>,H<sub>j</sub>_ into the input spaces of _S<sub>j</sub>_ and linear decoders _D<sub>j</sub>_ from the output space of _S<sub>j</sub>_ to that of _T_, satisfying

\(\sum_{j=1}^\alpha D_j(S_j(E_j(X),H_j(Y)))=T(X,Y)\) (2)

for all inputs (_X,Y_) of _T_. It is _same-left_ if every _E<sub>j</sub>_ is the identity. A packing _modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) allows coefficients in \(\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]\) in the linear maps and replaces (2) by \(Z_\varepsilon=T+\varepsilon R_\varepsilon\), where \(Z_\varepsilon\) is the decoded map and \(R_\varepsilon\) is bilinear with coefficients in \(\mathbb{Q}[\varepsilon]\).

We write \(D(W_1,\dots,W_\alpha)=\sum_{j=1}^\alpha D_j(W_j)\) for the combined decoder. For a list of independent targets, take _T_(**A**,**B**)=(_T<sub>i</sub>(A<sub>i</sub>,B<sub>i</sub>_))_<sub>i</sub>_; for a same-left list, take _T(A,_**B**)=(_T<sub>i</sub>(A,B<sub>i</sub>_))_<sub>i</sub>_. If all sources equal _S_, we say that the packing uses \(\alpha\) copies of _S_. Packings of polynomial products or their coefficient windows are _polynomial packings_ (PP); SL-PP denotes the same-left case. The parameter \(\varepsilon\) is distinct from the polynomial variables.

We recall two standard closure properties of bilinear algorithms: composition and combination on separate indices; see \[BCS97, Chapters 14-15\]. We give proofs in our notation for completeness.

When replacing a source computation by a packing, we use a sufficiently high power of \(\varepsilon\) in the replacement to preserve correctness modulo \(\varepsilon\).

**Lemma 2.2** (Composition)**.** _Suppose T has a packing modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _using_ \(S_1,\dots,S_\alpha\)_, and each S<sub>j</sub> has a packing modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _using_ \(R_{j,1},\dots,R_{j,\beta_j}\)_. For a computable positive integer K, replacing each source S<sub>j</sub> by its packing with_ \(\varepsilon\) _replaced by_ \(\varepsilon^K\) _gives a packing of T modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _using_ (_R<sub>j,k</sub>)<sub>j,k</sub>._

_Proof._ Choose nonnegative integers _p<sub>E</sub>,p<sub>H</sub>,p<sub>D</sub>_ so that the powers of \(\varepsilon\) in the coefficients of the left encoders, right encoders, and decoders of the packing of _T_ have exponents at least -_p<sub>E</sub>,-p<sub>H</sub>,-p<sub>D</sub>_, respectively. Choose _K=p<sub>E</sub>+p<sub>H</sub>+p<sub>D</sub>_+1. Each replacement has decoded error divisible by \(\varepsilon^K\). Billinearity shows that applying the outer encoders and decoders can lower its exponent by at most _p<sub>E</sub>+p<sub>H</sub>+p<sub>D</sub>_, so every added error remains divisible by \(\varepsilon\). The original decoded map is already congruent to _T_ modulo \(\varepsilon\), and the composite encoders and decoders are linear.

We also combine computations on separate coefficient indices. For maps _F,G_ with coefficient arrays _f,g_, their _tensor product_ is the bilinear map defined by \((F\otimes G)(X,Y)_{k,k^\prime}=\sum_{i,j,i^\prime,j^\prime} f_{ijk}g_{i^\prime j^\prime k^\prime} X_{i,i^\prime} Y_{j,j^\prime}\).

**Lemma 2.3** (Combining separate indices)**.** _If F has a packing using_ \(S_1,\dots,S_\alpha\) _and G has a packing using_ \(R_1,\dots,R_\beta\)_, then_ \(F\otimes G\) _has a packing using_ \((S_j\otimes R_k)_{j,k}\)_, obtained by encoding along the two indices and decoding in reverse order. The conclusion holds also modulo the same parameter_ \(\varepsilon\).

_Proof._ Abbreviating each list of sources, the correctness identities are

\(D(S(E(X),H(Y)))=F(X,Y),D'(R(E'(X),H'(Y)))=G(X,Y).\)

Expand the combined computation and group its sums by the unprimed indices. The primed encoding, computation, and decoding form the second identity; substitute it. Applying the first identity to each remaining term gives coefficient \(f_{ijk}g_{i^\prime j^\prime k^\prime}\). This uses only finite sums and linearity of the encoders and decoders. Modulo \(\varepsilon\), make the same substitutions with the complete decoded maps: their polynomial coefficient arrays multiply, and their constant coefficients are _f_ and _g_.

In particular, combining matrix multiplications of dimensions (_p,q,r_) and \((p',q',r')\) gives dimensions \((pp',qq',rr')\): the row, inner, and column indices are respectively paired. Appendix A gives the other operation we use, exchanging the input and output roles of a packing.

## 2.2 The primal and dual gadgets

Our first packing extends the three-for-one gadget of \[Ope26a, Lemma 4.2\]. It computes _c_+1 full products and one middle product from _c_ full products, allowing _t_ additional coefficients in each source right input. For _t_=1, this adds just one coefficient; larger _t_ permits smaller _c_.

Throughout the polynomial constructions, write _s=a+b_-1 and define

\(\mathrm{Full}_{a,b}(A,B)=AB,\mathrm{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q)=\big([z^{a-1+j}](AQ)\big)_{j=0}^{b-1},\)

where the lengths of _A,B,Q_ are _a,b,s_, respectively. Full returns _s_ coefficients, and Mid returns the _b_ coefficients at exponents _a_-1_,...,s_-1.

**Lemma 2.4** (Primal packing)**.** _For positive integers a,b,c,t with_ \(ct\ge a+2b-1\)_, there is a same-left packing modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _of_

\(\big((\mathrm{Full}_{a,b}(A,P_i))_{i=1}^{c+1},\mathrm{Mid}_{a,b}(A,Q)\big)\)

_using c copies of_ Full<sub>_a,b+t_</sub>_. Target and source coefficient sizes are_ \(p\times q,q\times r\) _for arbitrary positive integers p,q,r._

_Proof._ We are given _A_ of length _a_, polynomials _P_<sub>1</sub>_,...,P_<sub>_c_+1</sub> of length _b_, and _Q_ of length _s_. We will encode only the right inputs, multiply the encoded polynomials by the unchanged _A_, and recover the requested coefficients from these products.

## Encoding procedure.

Since \(ct\ge s+b>s\), we can split the coefficient list of _Q_ into _c_ consecutive blocks of length _t_, padding with zeros:<tbc>

\(Q^{(j)}(z)=\sum_{v=0}^{t-1}[z^{t(j-1)+v}]Qz^v,Q(z)=\sum_{j=1}^cz^{t(j-1)}Q^{(j)}(z).\)

<tbc>For \(1\le j\le c\), set

\(E_j=P_j-z^tP_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^bQ^{(j)}.\)

The first two terms combine adjacent right inputs using a shift of _t_. The last term places one block of \(\varepsilon Q\) in positions _b,...,b+t_-1. All three terms have degree less than _b+t_, so each _E<sub>j</sub>_ is a valid right input to Full<sub>_a,b+t_</sub>.

Compute the _c_ full source products _W<sub>j</sub>=AE<sub>j</sub>_, each of length _s+t_.

## Decoding procedure.

From these products, form the following telescoping sum:

\(W=\sum_{j=1}^cz^{t(j-1)}W_j=\sum_{j=1}^cz^{t(j-1)}AP_j-\sum_{j=1}^cz^{tj}AP_{j+1}+\varepsilon z^bA\sum_{j=1}^cz^{t(j-1)}Q^{(j)}=AP_1+\varepsilon z^bAQ-z^{ct}AP_{c+1}.\text{(3)}\)

In coefficient notation, this means computing

\([z^k]W=\sum_{j=1}^c[z^{k-t(j-1)}]W_j,\)

so forming _W_ is a fixed linear operation on the source outputs. For each \(2\le j\le c\), the term _z_<sup>_t(j_-1)</sup>_AP<sub>j</sub>_ occurs once with each sign and cancels. Only the two endpoint products remain, while the blocks of _Q_ reassemble into _Q_.

## Recover the middle product.

The first endpoint product _AP_<sub>1</sub> has no coefficients at exponents _s_ or above. The last endpoint product _z<sup>ct</sup>AP_<sub>_c_+1</sub> has no coefficients below \(ct\ge s+b\). Thus neither contributes at exponents _s,...,s+b_-1. For \(0\le k<b\), we obtain

\(\varepsilon^{-1}[z^{s+k}]W=[z^{s+k-b}](AQ)=[z^{a-1+k}](AQ).\)

These are exactly the _b_ coefficients of Mid<sub>_a,b_</sub>(_A,Q_). The division by \(\varepsilon\) is exact: every extracted coefficient has a factor \(\varepsilon\), and the resulting output is independent of \(\varepsilon\).

## Recover the full products.

First take the first _s_ coefficients of _W_:

\(Z_1=\sum_{k=0}^{s-1}[z^k]Wz^k.\)

Equation (3) gives \(Z_1\equiv AP_1(\mathrm{mod}\varepsilon)\): the final endpoint product does not reach this range, and the contribution from _Q_ is divisible by \(\varepsilon\). Once _Zj_ is known, subtract _Wj_, discard the first _t_ coefficients, and take the next _s_ coefficients. \(u=c^{2d},w=\left\lfloor\frac{(c+2)^{2d}}{d+1}\right\rfloor.\) (4)

\(\left(F_{a,b,I_i}(A,B_i)\right)_{i=1}^w\)

_Proof._ We begin with a common left input _A_ and an entire array of right inputs. Label the primal packing’s _c_+1 Full outputs and one Mid output by the letters of P in Lemma 2.6, and label the dual packing’s one Full output and _c_+1 Mid outputs by the letters of D. Index the array by words whose first _d_ letters lie in P and whose last _d_ letters lie in D. The letter at position _k_ specifies the local output in variable _z<sub>k</sub>_. A right input has length _b_ where its word has a Full letter and length _s_ where it has a Mid letter. There are (_c_+2)<sup>2_d_</sup> such positions; their right inputs are arbitrary and need not factor across variables.

### Encoding.

Compress this array one variable at a time, in the order _z_<sub>1</sub>_,...,z_<sub>2_d_</sub>. For _d_=1, write _x=z_<sub>1</sub> and _y=z_<sub>2</sub>. Write the inputs as _B<sub>i,j</sub>(x,y_), where _i_ labels a primal output and _j_ a dual output. Fix _j_, and expand \(B_{i,j}(x,y)=\sum_vB_{i,j,v}(x)y^v\). For each _v_, apply the primal encoder to the _c_+2 polynomials _B_<sub>1_,j,v_</sub>(_x),...,B_<sub>_c_+2_,j,v_</sub>(_x_). If the results are _U_<sub>1_,j,v_</sub>(_x),...,U_<sub>_c,j,v_</sub>(_x_), reassemble \(U_{r,j}(x,y)=\sum_vU_{r,j,v}(x)y^v\). Then expand each _U<sub>r,j</sub>_ in powers of _x_, apply the dual encoder to its lists of _y_-polynomials, and reassemble again.

For more variables, use their monomials in place of _y<sup>v</sup>_ in this same operation. At step _k_, denote the resulting list by **B**<sup>(_k_)</sup>, with **B**<sup>(0)</sup> the original array. Each step replaces one list index of size _c_+2 by one of size _c_. A processed variable has length _b+t_ if it is among the first _d_, and _s+t_ if it is among the last _d_. All other length bounds remain unchanged: they depend only on their own list indices, which are fixed while the current encoder runs. Thus every subsequent encoder receives lists with exactly the lengths required by its univariate packing. After 2_d_ steps there are _u_ right inputs, all in the domain of \(F_{a,b+t}^{(d)}\).

### Computation and decoding.

For two variables, let _E<sub>x</sub>,E<sub>y</sub>_ be the primal and dual encoders, and _D<sub>x</sub>,D<sub>y</sub>_ their decoders. Let _S_ denote the list of _c_<sup>2</sup> source products, and let _F<sub>i,j</sub>_ request the Full/Mid ranges specified by position (_i,j_). Lemma 2.3 combines the two univariate correctness identities to give

\([D_x(D_y(S(A,E_y(E_x(\mathbf{B}))))]_{i,j}\equiv F_{i,j}(A,B_{i,j})(\mathrm{mod}\varepsilon).\)

Thus encoding in _x_ and then _y_, computing the source products, and decoding in reverse order recovers the requested product at each position.

For 2_d_ variables, apply the same argument successively. Writing _E<sub>k</sub>,D<sub>k</sub>_ for the maps of step _k_, set

\(E=E_{2d}\circ\cdots\circ E_1,D=D_1\circ\cdots\circ D_{2d}.\)

Now let _S_ denote the list of _u_ source products. Compute _S(A,E_(**B**)) and apply _D_. Every requested output is recovered modulo \(\varepsilon\).

### Counting targets of the common shape.

Each recovered output is indexed by one word. Its Full set _I_ consists of the positions occupied by Full letters. Thus the outputs with |_I_|=_d_ correspond exactly to the words counted in Lemma 2.6, which gives at least (_c_+2)<sup>2_d_</sup>/(_d_+1) such outputs. Order each alphabet as displayed in that lemma, enumerate these words in lexicographic order, and keep the first _w_. Their Full sets are _I_<sub>1</sub>_,...,I<sub>w</sub>_; different words may have the same Full set. Put the prescribed _B<sub>i</sub>_ in these positions and zero in all other positions, then return the corresponding decoded outputs. The enumeration depends only on _c,d_.

The source Full set is always _I_<sub>0</sub>, but the target Full sets _I<sub>i</sub>_ may differ. Renaming a target into canonical form would also rename _A_. We therefore separate the left inputs before making these individual changes of variables.

## 2.4 Independent left inputs and a common target

We next give each target its own left input. We encode all left inputs in one univariate polynomial and each group of right inputs in its own univariate polynomial. The right inputs in group _i_ are encoded at the points \(i+\varepsilon j\). At each of these points, the left polynomial evaluates to _A<sub>i</sub>_ modulo \(\varepsilon\). This lets one interpolated product recover the entire group modulo \(\varepsilon\). Each target right input<tbc>

has _M_ column blocks; we recover the _M_<sup>2</sup> narrow output blocks using 2_M_-1 applications of the same-left packing.

**Lemma 2.8** (Separating left inputs)**.** _Let M,N,u,p,q,r be positive integers with_ \(M\ge 2\)_, and let F_<sub>0</sub>_,...,F_<sub>_M_-1</sub>_,S be maps of the form_ (1)_. Suppose a same-left packing modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _computes_ \((F_i(A,B_i))_{i=0}^{M-1}\) _on coefficient sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times r\) _using N copies of S on sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times ur\)_. Assume the F<sub>i</sub> have the same left-input space. Then a packing modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _computes_ \((F_i(A_i,B_i))_{i=0}^{M-1}\) _on sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times Mr\) _using N_(2_M_-1) _copies of S on sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times ur\).<sup>3</sup>

_Proof._ Given independent pairs _A<sub>i</sub>,B<sub>i</sub>_, write<tbc>

\(B_i=[B_{i,0}\cdots B_{i,M-1}],\)

<tbc>splitting every \(q\times Mr\) coefficient matrix horizontally into _M_ blocks of size \(q\times r\). Since _F<sub>i</sub>_ applies the same coefficient formula to each column block,

\(F_i(A_i,B_i)=[F_i(A_i,B_{i,0})\cdots F_i(A_i,B_{i,M-1})].\)

Thus we must recover all _M_ output blocks in each group _i_.

_Encode._ Interpolate one input-valued polynomial \(A(\xi)\) of degree at most _M_-1 with _A(i_)=_A<sub>i</sub>_. For each group _i_, interpolate a right-input-valued polynomial _C<sub>i</sub>(v_) of degree at most _M_-1 with _C<sub>i</sub>(j_)=_B<sub>i,j</sub>_, and define<tbc>

\(B'_i(\xi)=C_i\big(\frac{\xi-i}{\varepsilon}\big).\)

<tbc>The division by \(\varepsilon\) preserves the distinct right inputs as their interpolation points approach _i_:

\(B'_i(i+\varepsilon j)=C_i(j)=B_{i,j}(0\le j<M).\)

Meanwhile, _A_ is independent of \(\varepsilon\), so \(A(i+\varepsilon j)\equiv A_i(mod\varepsilon)\). We substitute \(\xi=i+\varepsilon j\) before taking the constant term: the coefficients of \(B'_i\) may contain negative powers of \(\varepsilon\). The points \(i,i+\varepsilon,\dots,i+\varepsilon(M-1)\) are distinct over \(\mathbb{Q}(\varepsilon)\). Since _C<sub>i</sub>_ has degree at most _M_-1, the coefficients of \(B'_i\) are Laurent polynomials in \(\varepsilon\) whose powers have exponents at least -(_M_-1). Both encodings are linear in their respective inputs.

_Compute and interpolate._ Consider the univariate polynomials

\(P_i(\xi)=F_i(A(\xi),B'_i(\xi)).\)

Bilinearity gives degree at most 2_M_-2 in \(\xi\). For each _k_=0_,...,_2_M_-2, use the given same-left packing to compute their values with common left input _A(k_) and right inputs \(B'_i(k)\). Replace the given packing’s parameter by \(\varepsilon^M\). Its decoded error is then divisible by \(\varepsilon^M\) before substituting the inputs. The left input contains no negative powers of \(\varepsilon\), and the powers in the right inputs have exponents at least -(_M_-1). Since the error is bilinear, after substitution it is still divisible by \(\varepsilon^{M-(M-1)}=\varepsilon\).

Interpolate the actual decoded values at these 2_M_-1 points. The interpolation coefficients are rational numbers independent of \(\varepsilon\), so the resulting polynomials satisfy<tbc>

\(\widetilde{P}_i(\xi)=P_i(\xi)+\varepsilon R_i(\xi,\varepsilon),\)

<sup>3</sup>The encoding at the points \(i+\varepsilon j\) in the proof was proposed by x after I prompted it to solve this separation problem using Reed-Muller decoding \[Sud02, Section 2.2\].

where _R<sub>i</sub>_ has polynomial coefficients in \(\xi,\varepsilon\).

_Decode._ For every block _j_ in group _i_, evaluate this same polynomial at \(\xi=i+\varepsilon j\). By the definition of \(B'_i\),

\(\widetilde{P}_i(i+\varepsilon j)=F_i(A(i+\varepsilon j),B_{i,j})+\varepsilon R_i(i+\varepsilon j,\varepsilon)\equiv F_i(A_i,B_{i,j})(\mathrm{mod}\varepsilon).\)

The last congruence follows from \(A(i+\varepsilon j)\equiv A(i)=A_i(\mathrm{mod}\varepsilon)\). Concatenating the recovered blocks gives _F<sub>i</sub>(A<sub>i</sub>,B<sub>i</sub>_) modulo \(\varepsilon\). Interpolation, evaluation, and concatenation are linear decoding maps. There are 2_M_-1 applications of the given packing, each using _N_ sources of the original sizes.

We apply this lemma after concatenating the same-left source products into one wider product. With independent left inputs, each target can then be put into the canonical Full set _I_<sub>0</sub>.

**Theorem 2.9** (Multivariate polynomial packing)**.** _Let c,d be positive integers, take u,w from_ (4)_, and put_ \(\alpha=2w-1\)_. _Proof._ Take the Full sets _I<sub>i</sub>_ and same-left packing from Lemma 2.7. ## 3 Reducing all matrix dimensions

We now turn the column reduction into a reduction in rows, inner dimension, and columns simultaneously. We also establish the \(a\leftrightarrow b\) symmetry and the terminal multiplication bound needed to compose these reductions.

## 3.1 Three roles

For a bilinear map _F_, the maps _F_<sup>(12)</sup> and _F_<sup>(13)</sup> exchange its two input roles and its left-input/output roles, respectively, as defined in Appendix A. Define

\(\widehat{F}=F\otimes F^{(12)}\otimes F^{(13)}.\)

The three factors act on separate coefficient indices. This construction allows the three matrix dimensions to be reduced by the same factor.

**Lemma 3.1** (Packing in all dimensions)**.** _Let_ \(M,\alpha,u,w\) _be positive integers and let F,S be maps of the form_ (1)_. Suppose a packing computes M independent copies of F on coefficient sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times wr\) _using_ \(\alpha\) _copies of S on sizes_ \(p\times q,q\times ur\)_, with the same scalar formulas for all compatible matrix blocks. Then M_<sup>3</sup> _copies of_ \(\widehat{F}\) _on sizes_

\(pw\times qw,qw\times rw\)

_can be packed into_ \(\alpha^3\) _copies of_ \(\widehat{S}\) _on sizes_ \(pu\times qu,qu\times ru\)_. The implication holds modulo_ \(\varepsilon\) _as well._

_Proof._ The given reduction changes the matrix-dimension triple (_p,q,wr_) to (_p,q,ur_). Its (12) role exchange gives \((pw,q,r)\longrightarrow(pu,q,r)\), and its (13) exchange gives \((p,qw,r)\longrightarrow(p,qu,r)\), by Lemma A.1. Combine the three packings on separate coefficient groups and on the column, row, and inner block indices, respectively. Lemma 2.3 multiplies their target and source counts and gives the claimed sizes, leaving the outer block dimensions _p,q,r_ unchanged.

## 3.2 Symmetry and terminal evaluation

For the remainder of the proof let \(G_{a,b}=\widehat{F_{a,b}^{(d)}}\), with _d_ fixed. The preceding lemma and Theorem 2.9 give a packing of _w_<sup>3</sup> copies of _G<sub>a,b</sub>_ into \(\alpha^3\) copies of _G<sub>a,b+t</sub>_. We first show that exchanging _a,b_ lets us apply this packing to either length parameter.

**Lemma 3.2** (Symmetry)**.** _For all positive integers a,b, exchanging a and b in G<sub>a,b</sub> amounts to fixed reorderings of the coefficients of its inputs and output; the coefficient-matrix sizes remain unchanged._

_Proof._ Put _s=a+b_-1. Reverse the output coefficient index in Full and Mid, carrying this reversal along when exchanging roles. The six groups defining _G<sub>a,b</sub>_ then contain all six orders of the lengths (_a,b,s_), each repeated _d_ times, with the common coefficient condition _i+j+k=s_-1. Exchanging _a,b_ simply permutes these groups. Undoing the coefficient reversals gives the asserted reordering.

We next bound the cost of finishing the polynomial computation with ordinary matrix multiplication.

**Lemma 3.3** (Terminal evaluation)**.** _We have G_<sub>1,1</sub>(_A,B_)=_AB. For every positive integer L, G<sub>L,L</sub> can be computed exactly using O(L_<sup>6_d_</sup>) _matrix multiplications of the original coefficient sizes._

_Proof._ At _a=b_=1, every coefficient list has length one, giving _AB_.

For _a=b=L_, the product of two scalar length-_L_ polynomials has degree _O(L_). Standard evaluation and interpolation \[BCS97, Chapter 14\] computes Full using _O(L_) scalar products: evaluate at _O(L_) distinct rational points, multiply the values, and interpolate. Exchanging the right-input and output roles and reversing the left coefficient list gives Mid. Further role exchanges preserve this product count. Combine these algorithms over the 6_d_ coefficient directions, then substitute matrix coefficients, using Lemma 2.3. The result uses _O(L_<sup>6_d_</sup>) matrix products of the original sizes.

## 4 A fixed matrix multiplication identity

We now compose the packing in both length parameters. Each round shrinks the coefficient matrices and increases the polynomial lengths; the terminal bound in Lemma 3.3 accounts for the cost of those longer polynomials.

### 4.1 Construction of the identity

The next theorem produces a single finite rational identity. Once its parameters have been fixed, ordinary block recursion will apply it to matrices of arbitrary size.

**Theorem 4.1** (A fixed identity)**.** _For every_ \(\tau>9/4\)_, there are computable integers_ \(v,r\ge 2\) _with_ \(r<v^\tau\)_, rational linear forms_ \(\ell_\nu,m_\nu\) _on_ \(v\times v\) _matrices, and rational matrices_ \(W_\nu\in\mathbb{Q}^{v\times v}\) _such that_<tbc>

\(AB=\sum_{\nu=1}^r\ell_\nu(A)m_\nu(B)W_\nu(A,B\in\mathbb{Q}^{v\times v}).\) (6)

<tbc>_Proof._ Fix \(c\ge 2\), to be chosen sufficiently large, and take _d=c_<sup>3</sup>, _u,w_ from (4), and \(\alpha=2w-1\). Set

\(R=\lfloor w/u\rfloor^2,\rho=1+\frac{3}{c-1}.\)

We have _w\>_2_u_, \(R\ge 4\), and log_R_=8_c_<sup>2</sup>+_O(c_) by (5).

### One round.

Given _w_<sup>3</sup> products of _G<sub>L,L</sub>_ with square coefficient matrices of side _w_<sup>2</sup>_Rn_, put

\(t=\left\lceil\frac{3L-1}{c-1}\right\rceil,L'=L+t\le\rho L+1.\)

The condition \(ct\ge a+2b-1\) holds both at (_a,b_)=(_L,L_) and at \((L',L)\), since \((c-1)t\ge 3L-1\). Theorem 2.9 and Lemma 3.1 first reduce the _w_<sup>3</sup> given products to \(\alpha^3\) products of \(G_{L,L^\prime}\) at matrix side _wuRn_. Use Lemma 3.2 to replace each by \(G_{L^\prime,L}\), permuting its coefficient lists and undoing the output permutation when decoding.

Since \(\alpha<2w\), put these products into eight batches of _w_<sup>3</sup>, padding with zero inputs. Apply the same packing to each batch. This gives at most \(8\alpha^3<64w^3\) products of \(G_{L^\prime,L^\prime}\) at matrix side \(u^2Rn\le w^2n\). Pad to side _w_<sup>2</sup>_n_ and to 64_w_<sup>3</sup> products. Lemma 2.2 composes the two steps modulo one parameter. Thus a round divides the matrix side by _R_, multiplies the product count by at most 64, and changes _L_ to at most \(\rho L+1\).

### Iteration.

Start one matrix product of side _v<sub>k</sub>=w_<sup>2</sup>_R<sup>k</sup>_ in a list of _w_<sup>3</sup> products of _G_<sub>1,1</sub>, with zero inputs in the other positions. After _k_ rounds there are at most _w_<sup>3</sup>64_<sup>k</sup>_ products of _G<sub>L<sub>k</sub>,L<sub>k</sub></sub>_ at matrix side _w_<sup>2</sup>, where<tbc>

\(L_0=1,L_k\le\rho^k+\frac{\rho^k-1}{\rho-1}=O_c(\rho^k).\)

<tbc>Finish each using Lemma 3.3, and compute the remaining fixed-size matrix products by the elementary algorithm. Repeated use of Lemma 2.2 gives a packing modulo \(\varepsilon\) for the original matrix product with at most<tbc>

\(r_k=O_c\big((64\rho^{6d})^k\big)\)

<tbc>scalar products. Its exponent satisfies

\(\frac{\mathrm{log}(64\rho^{6d})}{\mathrm{log}R}=\frac{18c^2+O(c)}{8c^2+O(c)}=\frac{9}{4}+O(1/c).\)

Choose _c_ so that \(64\rho^{6d}<R^\tau\), and then _k_ so that \(r_k<v_k^\tau\). These choices are finite and effective.

### Removing the formal parameter.

Since \(r_k<v_k^\tau\), Bini’s approximate-to-exact lemma \[Bin80\], stated and proved for completeness as Lemma B.1, converts this packing into an exact rational identity (6) at a computable finite side _v_, using \(r<v^\tau\) scalar products. All coefficients arise from the stated encodings, permutations, and rational interpolations.

The choice _d=c_<sup>3</sup> gives convergence 9/4+_O_(1_/c_). One can instead take _d=c_<sup>2</sup>: then log_R_=8_c+O_(log_c_) and \(\mathrm{log}(64\rho^{6d})=18c+O(1)\), giving 9/4+_O_(log_c/c_). This uses 6_c_<sup>2</sup> rather than 6_c_<sup>3</sup> polynomial variables, at the cost of slower convergence.

## 4.2 Integer arithmetic

We finish by applying standard block recursion to the fixed identity, as in Strassen’s algorithm \[Str69\]. Its parameters and coefficients are constants once the requested exponent is fixed.

_Proof of Theorem 1.1._ Choose the identity in Theorem 4.1 with \(\tau=9/4+\gamma\). This identity also holds for matrix blocks: expanding both sides gives the same coefficient for every ordered product of a left-input block and a right-input block. Clear the fixed denominators in the encoders and decoder to obtain integer linear maps whose decoded output is \(\delta AB\) for a fixed positive integer \(\delta\).

For _n=v<sup>j</sup>_, partition the input matrices into \(v\times v\) blocks, encode, recursively multiply the _r_ encoded pairs, decode, and divide every output entry exactly by \(\delta\). All operations outside the recursive products cost _O(n_<sup>2</sup>), so

\(T(n)\le rT(n/v)+O(n^2)=O(n^\tau),\)

since \(r<v^\tau\) and \(\tau>2\). Padding to the next power of _v_ handles every positive integer _n_.

For _B_-bit integer inputs, encoding adds only _O_(1) bits per level. Products have at most twice the resulting input length, and decoding adds _O_(log_n_) bits over the remaining levels. All intermediate integers therefore have _O(B_+log_n_) bits. The bit cost is \(O(n^{9/4+\gamma}\mathsf{M}(B+\mathrm{log}n))\), where M(_b_) is the cost of multiplying _b_-bit integers; multiplication and exact division by the fixed constants take linear time.

By the definition of a packing modulo \(\varepsilon\), the coefficients of the fully decoded map are polynomials with no negative powers, and their constant terms are the coefficients of matrix multiplication. Each coefficient of the combined decoded map is a product of _h_ such polynomials. Its degree is therefore at most _hD_, and its constant term is the product of their constant terms.
